a4af93e58fe29ed7: MELAKA: Menteri Pengangkutan Loke Siew Fook menafikan bantuan khas kewangan sebanyak RM1,000 yang diberikan kepada pemandu teksi, kereta sewa dan bas sekolah di Melaka pada hari ini bertujuan 'memancing undi' bersempena dengan PRN Melaka.

Beliau berkata sebaliknya, insentif berkenaan diberikan kepada semua pemandu teksi, kereta sewa dan bas sekolah di seluruh negara selepas diumumkan oleh Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim ketika membentangkan Belanjawan 2027 di Parlimen, baru-baru ini.

"Saya nak betulkan beberapa kenyataan dekat luar, ada yang tanya mengapa hanya di Melaka? Hakikatnya (pemberian bantuan khas kewangan) ini untuk semua pemandu teksi di seluruh negara, bukan di Melaka sahaja.

"Hari ini, saya (sampaikan bantuan khas kewangan) di Melaka, minggu lepas saya di Negeri Sembilan, minggu depan saya pergi Kedah pula, jadi di setiap negeri seluruh negara, pemandu teksi dan kereta sewa juga akan mendapat bantuan khas ini," katanya.

Beliau berkata demikian ketika ditemui pemberita selepas merasmikan Majlis Pemberian Bantuan Khas Kewangan kepada Pemandu Teksi, Kereta Sewa dan Bas Sekolah di Auditorium Kompleks CMI, Ayer Keroh, di sini hari ini.
Sebanyak 283 pemandu teksi dan kereta sewa menerima baucar sumbangan bernilai RM1,000 setiap seorang pada majlis tersebut.

Mengulas lanjut, Loke berkata pada minggu ini sahaja, terdapat kira-kira 12,000 pemandu teksi, kereta sewa dan bas sekolah akan menerima bantuan khas kewangan tersebut bagi meringankan beban ditanggung mereka.

"Yang tidak sempat kita jemput untuk majlis, kita buat pemindahan ataupun bank-in melalui Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT). Bantuan ini tidak mengira tempat, selagi dia ada kad pemandu yang sah dan mereka sahkan kad pemandu itu dengan Agensi Pengangkutan Awam Darat (APAD), maka kita akan dapat daftar nama mereka dalam sistem dan akan diberi bantuan RM1,000.

"Bermula hari ini juga, ada lebih 12,000 nama yang akan kita kreditkan (bantuan khas kewangan) dalam akaun bank masing-masing … kita berharap bantuan ini dapat disalurkan secepat mungkin untuk meringankan beban mereka," katanya.
21a7c0dfb14091d7: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — Former Court of Appeal Judge Datuk Mahadev Shankar, renowned for his legal acumen, language mastery, and enduring contributions to Malaysian jurisprudence, died at Shah Alam Hospital at 2 am today. He was 94.
His close friend, Malaysia-India Heritage Society founder-president Prabhakaran Nair, said funeral arrangements would be announced later.
“Sadly, the Malaysia-India Heritage Society has lost a dear well-wisher whose friendship and goodwill we shall always cherish.

“His contributions to the Malaysian judiciary and involvement in the advancement of human rights, including his association with Suhakam (the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia), form an important part of his legacy,” he said.
Mahadev began his legal career in the 1950s and was appointed a High Court judge in August 1983 before being elevated to the Court of Appeal in 1994. He retired from the Bench in November 1997.

Born in Kuala Lumpur in 1932, Mahadev’s early exposure to the courts, coupled with a strong grounding in classical literature and languages, shaped a distinguished career spanning legal practice, judicial service and legal scholarship.

He began practising in Seremban before joining the law firm Shearn Delamore & Co, where he became a partner in 1961. He remained with the firm throughout his legal practice, handling a broad range of cases involving commercial and civil disputes, criminal law and medical negligence.

Mahadev was also recognised for his contributions to legal scholarship. An article he published in the Malayan Law Journal in 1984 on the distinction between putting a case to a witness and merely suggesting something to the witness continued to be cited by the Court of Appeal decades later.
His judgments covered issues ranging from employment disputes and damages in matrimonial cases to delays in the administration of justice.
In one ruling, he cautioned against delays that could leave litigants receiving their awards years later, when victory had become “academic or worse still pyrrhic”.
In a 2014 interview, he described judges as “tigers under the throne”, adapting a phrase traditionally associated with the judiciary’s role under the Crown to reflect the Malaysian context.

Some aspects of Mahadev’s legal career, scholarship and approach to the law were also highlighted by author and senior constitutional lawyer GK Ganesan in his article, ‘Is There Any Point in Learning Things by Heart’, in which he paid tribute to the late judge.

“He was one of the most learned men ever to sit on our Bench. Old English, Sanskrit, the Vedas, the whole of English literature: he knew them as other judges know their law reports. In that company, no judge in this country has equalled him,” Ganesan said. — Bernama
688f8d97c3f6872b: BRASILIA, Oct 26 — Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback yesterday as he clinched a re-election victory, but his rival Flavio Bolsonaro refused to accept the loss and said he would seek to annul the vote.
With Lula’s victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries — such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru — all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump.
The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied projections to win an unprecedented fourth term.
According to official results, he won 51.8 percent of the votes to 48.2 percent for Flavio Bolsonaro, with Lula pulling around 4.4 million more votes.
The senator is the son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year jail term for attempting a coup after his loss to Lula in the country’s last election in 2022.
Sunday’s vote was marked by confusion after a Supreme Court ruling extended voting by two hours as some polling stations had already closed.
The move came at the request of Lula who complained that buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting.
Flavio Bolsonaro also requested an extension in some regions due to heavy rains, but he described the decision as “unacceptable” and a “dirty trick”
“It is impossible to recognize the results. I am going to request the annulment of these elections,” he said, stone-faced, in a brief speech in Brasilia.
No candidate who lost the first round has gone on to win the second in Brazil since 1989, the first direct election after the end of the country’s military dictatorship.
“People went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important for ensuring democracy in the country,” Lula said in his first comments after the win.
Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula’s Workers’ Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate.
Lula’s fight back
After the first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies, declaring “Never Again Bolsonaro” and revamped their social media strategy.
The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21 percent to 19 percent.
Julio Canelo, 42, a lawyer celebrating in Rio de Janeiro hailed a victory for “the entire democratic spectrum.”
“It was the result of the people mobilizing, in the streets and online,” he told AFP.
A fierce social media battle drew in Meta, parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, which Lula’s campaign accused of favoring his opponent with “algorithmic manipulation.”
Meta denied this but acknowledged that some of Lula’s campaign ads had been mistakenly deactivated due to technical errors.
“We are going to have to regulate them,” Lula said of social media companies after his win.
A bitter campaign marred by scandals and mudslinging laid bare the deep divisions that have plagued Brazil over the past decade.
A country split in two
Lula heads into a fourth term with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change.
He rose from poverty to become president in 2003 and was re-elected in 2006.
Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.
The charges were annulled on procedural grounds.
In his third term, Lula oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters felt gloomy about the high cost of living and crime.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, pitched himself as more moderate and jovial than his father and managed to galvanize conservatives as well as less ideological voters wanting something new.
“We’re in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat — buying meat is out of the question,” said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro.
Already one of the world’s oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030.
He is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right.
Lula’s campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump’s United States.
“This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard,” he said Sunday.
Lula received congratulations from Chile’s far-right president, Jose Antonio Kast, and Ecuador’s right-wing Daniel Noboa — both close Trump allies.
Mexico’s left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum wrote on X, saying “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” — AFP
df81a3f70d727d15: IT people are asked to cram a lot into a working week, which is why The Register tries to ease readers into Monday with a new instalment of “Who, Me?” – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of office mistakes and escapes.
This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as "Robert," who told us he worked for an outfit that scours newspapers and websites to find stories mentioning their clients.
"We found key words in articles that customers were paying us to monitor for. We would then cut out the articles and send them to the customer," Robert explained.
Sadly, business wasn't great. By the time Robert left it was almost bankrupt, and he gathers a fire sale ensued.
That strained financial situation meant the company was very keen on keeping legacy hardware alive.
"We had this one 2U pizza box server, and one of the three internal fans wore out," Robert explained. The server was so old no replacement was available.
"So, we took the lid off and put a bigger fan on top of the component that needed the airflow," Robert confessed. The server couldn't tell the difference and kept working.
Six months later, another internal fan broke.
"The logical thing to do was to put another ill-fitted fan in/on the server to ensure that the airflow was good," Robert said. Again, the server didn’t have a problem with that.
The server, which was an integral part of the company’s daily operations, was now operating with one original fan, no lid, and two non-standard fans precariously balanced over its exposed components.
"We had to be careful when working near the server, because too much shaking would cause the fans to fall over," Robert confessed.
When the third internal fan died, management finally decided to buy a new box.

Have you rigged risky hardware and gotten away with it? If so, share your story by clicking here to send email to Who, Me? We're pretty sure The Register's hardware will hold together long enough for us to tell your tale on some future Monday. ®

62a80b9e01750f27: PETALING JAYA: An Indonesian environmental NGO plans to take legal action against Malaysian and Singaporean plantation companies allegedly involved in the recent transboundary haze.

The Indonesian Forum for the Environment (Walhi) today outlined its plans to sue Singaporean companies in a Jakarta district court, saying it is also considering filing lawsuits directly in Singapore, targeting holding companies rather than just their Indonesian subsidiaries.

"We are still discussing this with consultants, and we will hire an international lawyer to help build our case against holding companies in Singapore," Walhi campaign coordinator Uli Arta Siagian said at a roundtable hosted by Malaysian advocacy group Monitoring Sustainability of Globalisation (MSN).
Uli said the NGO was still developing its legal arguments and gathering data on the extent of Malaysian companies’ alleged involvement in the forest fires that have contributed to the haze.
She said one obstacle to holding companies accountable was the lack of a strong Asean legal framework to address transboundary haze pollution.

A 2022 Walhi report found that the 2002 Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution lacked an enforcement mechanism, relying instead on member states to consult and negotiate when haze affects other countries.

MSN director Charles Santiago said Singapore faced similar challenges in 2015 when it sought information from Indonesian local authorities about forest fires under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.
"Given that there was no response, there was no basis to file a charge even against companies from their own country, so it just collapsed," he said.

When asked about media reports that Malaysian companies were not included on a list of firms identified by the Indonesian government as responsible for the haze, Walhi urged Putrajaya to conduct a proper investigation rather than assume that no Malaysian companies were involved.

Fires in Indonesia have blanketed parts of Southeast Asia in toxic smoke, forcing school closures, driving up respiratory illnesses and curtailing outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and Timor-Leste.

Earlier this month, government spokesman Fahmi Fadzil said most of the fires observed in Indonesia occurred outside oil palm concessions owned by Malaysian companies, according to checks with the firms.
04606b85f69a57ef: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — The permanent disposal facility (PDF) for radioactive waste generated by Lynas Malaysia Sdn Bhd had achieved 77 per cent completion in construction and operations as of Aug 31, with 1.45 million metric tonnes of the 1.467 million metric tonnes of Water Leach Purification (WLP) waste generated having been transferred to the facility.

Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Datuk Chang Lih Kang said four disposal cells, designated A, B, C and D, had been completed, while the process of filling the facility with Auto Leach Residue (ALR) waste was ongoing.

“Based on monitoring by the Atomic Energy Department (JTA) up to Sept 10, radiation dose readings outside the PDF were also below 20 millisieverts per year, complying with the dose limit stipulated under Act 304 (Atomic Energy Licensing Act 1984) for radiation workers,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat today.

He was responding to a question from Chow Yu Hui (PH-Raub) on the justification for renewing Lynas’ licence for 10 years, the status of the PDF, the amount of accumulated radioactive waste, and the mechanisms in place to ensure the company stops generating radioactive waste by 2031 and complies with all licence conditions.

Chang said Lynas was required to stop generating WLP radioactive waste before March 2031, while existing waste and waste generated during the period must be treated to reduce its activity concentration to below one becquerel (Bq) per gram using methods proven effective through research and development (R&D).
“This approach aims to reduce and eventually stop the generation of radioactive waste through recycling or reuse, while ensuring that mineral resources are managed sustainably and safely,” he said.

On who would be responsible in the event of a radioactive waste leak, Chang said Lynas was required to monitor the facility within the Lynas Advanced Materials Plant (LAMP) site during the first five years.
This was to ensure that the activity concentration of WLP waste could be reduced to below the control limit of one becquerel per gram stipulated under Act 304.

“Lynas must also continue its R&D on WLP waste, which will be monitored by the JTA. After the five years, if Lynas is still generating radioactive WLP waste, the JTA may suspend or revoke the licence.
“Therefore, the JTA will be responsible for ensuring that Lynas ceases generating radioactive waste by March 2031,” he said.

In March, the government decided to renew Lynas Rare Earths’ operating licence for another 10 years, allowing the Australian mining company to import raw materials containing naturally occurring radioactive materials and process rare earth elements (REE). — Bernama
d044fe079945f357: KUALA LUMPUR: Former Court of Appeal judge Mahadev Shankar, known for his legal acumen, language mastery and contributions to Malaysian jurisprudence, died at Shah Alam Hospital at 2am today. He was 94.
His close friend, Malaysia-India Heritage Society founder-president N Prabhakaran, said funeral arrangements would be announced later.

"His contributions to the Malaysian judiciary and involvement in the advancement of human rights, including his association with Suhakam (the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia), form an important part of his legacy," he said.
Mahadev began his legal career in the 1950s and was appointed a High Court judge in August 1983 before being elevated to the Court of Appeal in 1994. He retired from the bench in November 1997.

Born in Kuala Lumpur in 1932, Mahadev's early exposure to the courts, coupled with a strong grounding in classical literature and languages, shaped a distinguished career spanning legal practice, judicial service and legal scholarship.

He began practising in Seremban before joining the law firm Shearn Delamore & Co, where he became a partner in 1961. He remained with the firm throughout his legal practice, handling a broad range of cases involving commercial and civil disputes, criminal law and medical negligence.

Mahadev was also recognised for his contributions to legal scholarship. An article he published in the Malayan Law Journal in 1984 on the distinction between putting a case to a witness and merely suggesting something to the witness continues to be cited by the Court of Appeal, decades later.
His judgments covered issues ranging from employment disputes and damages in matrimonial cases to delays in the administration of justice.
In one ruling, he cautioned against delays that could leave litigants receiving their awards years later, when victory had become "academic or, worse still, pyrrhic".
In a 2014 interview, he described judges as "tigers under the throne", adapting a phrase traditionally associated with the judiciary's role under the Crown to reflect the Malaysian context.

Some aspects of Mahadev's legal career, scholarship and approach to the law were also highlighted by author and senior constitutional lawyer GK Ganesan in his article, "Is There Any Point in Learning Things by Heart", in which he paid tribute to the late judge.

"He was one of the most learned men ever to sit on our bench. Old English, Sanskrit, the Vedas, the whole of English literature: he knew them as other judges know their law reports. In that company, no judge in this country has equalled him," Ganesan said.
236989345c2bc950: KUALA LUMPUR: Negeri SG4 terbuka menjadi perintis bagi kajian penggunaan teknologi nuklear baharu seperti reaktor modular kecil (SMR) di Malaysia sebagai alternatif penjanaan tenaga pada masa depan, kata Pengerusi Perikatan Nasional, Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar.

"Kerajaan negeri perlu diberikan lebih banyak ruang untuk menentukan sendiri projek yang patut diberikan keutamaan, bukan segala-galanya ditentukan kerajaan persekutuan."
Beliau berkata, perkara itu antara aspek yang diharap boleh diubah jika gabungan politiknya berjaya menawan Putrajaya selepas PRU16.

Jelasnya, antara syarat belum dipenuhi membabitkan lesen pengendali aerodrom (AOL).

"Tiada garis masa (ditetapkan untuk kelulusan projek itu). Jika mereka (kerajaan persekutuan) tidak meluluskannya, maka ia tidak akan berlaku," katanya sambil menambah satu-satunya halangan ketika ini ialah proses kelulusan oleh Putrajaya memandangkan pelabur sudah bersiap sedia.

Jika Putrajaya tidak meluluskan projek itu sekarang, beliau berkata, Kedah perlu menunggu selepas PRU16 dengan harapan kerajaan persekutuan diambil alih gabungan lain untuk projek berkenaan direalisasikan.

b78d75f908986507: SINGAPORE, Oct 26 — Singapore will further its assessment on the feasibility of harnessing geothermal energy for power generation, cooling, and heating, said Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Dr Tan See Leng.

Announcing this at the Singapore Energy Lecture at the Singapore International Energy Week 2026 (SIEW) on Monday (Oct 26), Dr Tan pointed to the positive preliminary findings from a non-invasive geophysical survey last year.
The survey found that Singapore has high-temperature geothermal resources at depths of several kilometres underground, which may be suitable for electricity generation.
Its technical potential of geothermal energy for power generation is more than 60 times of the country’s annual electricity consumption of around 60 terawatt-hours (TWh).
In a media release issued after the lecture, the Energy Market Authority of Singapore (EMA) said the survey assessed that there are lower-temperature geothermal resources at shallower depths.
This could potentially support industrial heating and cooling using heat pumps and absorption chillers, it added.
However, the feasibility study of deploying next-generation geothermal power plants in Singapore is not a straightforward one, the energy and industry minister highlighted.

“Our geothermal resources are located several kilometres underground, the amount of electricity we can eventually generate will depend on the cost and technical feasibility of extracting these resources, as well as the pace of advances in deep drilling technology,” he said.
Dr Tan added that Singapore’s dense urban environment will also affect how many geothermal power plants it can feasibly deploy.
In addition, safety has to be the top-of-mind consideration for energy planners, the minister cautioned.

Now, following a request for proposal launched in April this year, EMA has appointed a consortium formed by Surbana Jurong and Canadian energy consulting group GLJ to conduct the next-phase of this feasibility study.
The study, expected to take about 15 months from the end of 2026, will cover safety considerations, technical viability, and the cost of geothermal energy production.

EMA chief executive Puah Kok Keong highlighted that geothermal energy is an indigenous source of clean energy that can provide constant power, and can potentially play an important role in the country’s energy mix.
“If proven to be viable for electricity generation, Singapore’s geothermal energy resources will strengthen our energy resilience and support the decarbonisation of the power sector,” he said.

EMA added that any decision to deploy geothermal will also be taken after further technical and feasibility studies are completed and will depend on the progress of technologies for deep geothermal energy.
The move is the latest in a series of energy-related announcements made at SIEW.
In his energy lecture, Dr Tan emphasised that energy is existential for Singapore.
“We must ensure that our system resilience continues to be a source of confidence for our people,” he said. — AsiaOne

09abc2a360748e5d: KUALA LUMPUR: The parliamentary service council can discuss equal allocations for MPs, anti-hopping laws and no-confidence motions, law and institutional reform minister Azalina Othman Said said today.
However, she made no commitment to changing the policies, saying the government would leave the matters to the council to discuss.

"On behalf of the government, we are leaving it to the parliamentary service council to discuss the way forward on these policy matters," she said when winding up the debate on the 2027 budget in the Dewan Rakyat.
She was responding to Ronald Kiandee (PN-Beluran), who asked for the government’s position on the three issues.
Ronald asked whether the council’s responsibilities should extend beyond Parliament’s administration to matters involving government policy.
"Would this not create a conflict between Parliament and the executive, given the broad scope of these responsibilities?" he said.

The council was established under the Parliamentary Service Act 2025, which took effect on Oct 1, to give Parliament greater control over its staff, finances and administration rather than relying on the government.
Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman (Muda-Muar) proposed that every MP receive at least RM400,000 a year to cover staff salaries, office rental and utility bills, with the funds managed by Parliament.

He said constituency allocations were currently controlled by the Prime Minister’s Office, raising questions about whether Parliament could administer the funds without them being transferred to its control.
Azalina said the council could consider the proposal, adding however that any changes would take time.
She said the council was expected to become fully operational after two Dewan Negara representatives were selected in early December.

The council currently comprises two MPs each from the government and opposition blocs: Ramkarpal Singh (PH-Bukit Gelugor), Hasni Mohammad (BN-Simpang Renggam), Ronald Kiandee (PN-Beluran) and Takiyuddin Hassan (PN-Kota Bharu).
On a separate matter, Azalina said she would chair a committee to study the proposed establishment of a Malaysian Law Reform Commission.
She said the government was considering whether the commission should operate as an independent body, like the Human Rights Commission of Malaysia, or come under Parliament’s purview.

The commission will review outdated laws, identify gaps in existing legislation and recommend amendments. The government is also studying whether it should be required to respond to the commission’s recommendations.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced plans to establish the commission when tabling the 2027 budget.
809b887a345610d3: TOKYO: Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, who used his brief period in office to seek closer ties with Asian neighbours, particularly China, has died at the age of 90, the Nikkei business daily reported on Monday.
The Japanese politician, the first son of a prime minister to become premier himself, died on Thursday from heart failure, the Nikkei said.
Becoming prime minister on the sudden resignation of Shinzo Abe in 2007, Fukuda lasted less than a year -- a tenure even shorter than his father Takeo's two-year stint.

A graduate in economics from Tokyo's prestigious Waseda University, Fukuda spent nearly two decades working his way up the ranks of an oil company -- including a two-year posting in the US -- before resigning to become a political secretary when his father became premier in 1976.

Elected to Japan's more powerful lower house of parliament in 1990, Fukuda was chief cabinet secretary from 2000 to 2004, resigning as one of several cabinet ministers to admit not paying into the pension system.
Known for his testy manner, the bespectacled Fukuda drew criticism in 2003 for off-the-record comments in which he suggested women who dressed provocatively were asking to be raped.
When Fukuda succeeded Abe he joked he might have drawn the short straw in assuming office given the divided parliament and opposition parties' ability to delay legislation.
Frustrated with the stalled legislative process, Fukuda resigned in 2008, the second of six prime ministers to quit after only around a year in office.
Known as a diplomatic dove, Fukuda made several visits to China after leaving office in an effort to improve often fraught relations.
Fukuda leaves a son, Tatsuo, who is also a lawmaker and has been viewed as a potential future prime minister.

Mahkamah Tinggi turut meneliti sifat fatwa itu, yang menurut alasan penghakiman ditujukan kepada pemimpin, pengikut, pekerja dan ahli GISBH beragama Islam.

Tetapi, GISBH dalam memorandum rayuannya mempertikaikan keputusan itu dengan berhujah cabarannya bukan bertujuan meminta mahkamah sivil menentukan persoalan hukum syarak, sebaliknya meneliti kesahan fatwa serta proses pengeluarannya.
Ia turut membangkitkan persoalan berhubung pelaksanaan fatwa terhadap entiti korporat seperti GISBH.
Pada 18 Okt 2024, Jawatankuasa Fatwa Selangor mengisytihar dan mewartakan GISBH menyeleweng daripada ajaran Islam, selain melarang orang Islam mengamalkan kepercayaan, ajaran serta doktrinnya.
547a7b6a478ae1cc: PUTRAJAYA: Mahkamah Rayuan mengurangkan ganti rugi RM117 juta yang diperintahkan terhadap Majlis Perbandaran Klang (MPK) kepada RM3 juta dalam pertikaian berhubung kerja pemulihan bekas tapak pelupusan sampah milik pihak berkuasa tempatan itu.

Panel tiga hakim diketuai Hakim Ismail Brahim bersama Hakim K Muniandy dan Dean Wayne Daly sebulat suara membenarkan rayuan MPK yang kini dikenali sebagai Majlis Bandaraya Diraja Klang, terhadap jumlah ganti rugi diberikan kepada pemaju hartanah NBC Land Sdn Bhd.

Mahkamah turut mengetepikan faedah sebelum penghakiman hampir RM50 juta yang diberikan Mahkamah Tinggi Shah Alam dan memerintahkan NBC Land membayar kos RM60,000 bagi prosiding rayuan serta penilaian ganti rugi.

Pertikaian itu berpunca daripada perjanjian bertarikh 2 Dis 2003 yang menetapkan kedua-dua pihak berkongsi sama rata anggaran kos RM6 juta untuk memulihkan tapak pelupusan berkenaan menggunakan kaedah menutup sisa dengan lapisan tanah.

Bagaimanapun, Mahkamah Tinggi menilai keseluruhan kos pemulihan sebanyak RM234 juta, termasuk kerja menggali dan mengalihkan hampir dua juta tan sisa serta menggantikannya dengan bahan tambakan kejuruteraan.
Majlis itu kemudian diperintahkan membayar separuh daripada jumlah tersebut, iaitu RM117 juta, berserta faedah.
Dalam membenarkan rayuan itu, Mahkamah Rayuan memutuskan penilaian tersebut melangkaui skop perjanjian asal antara kedua-dua pihak.
Muniandy berkata apa yang dipersetujui ialah menutup sisa dengan kira-kira 1.5m tanah yang dipadatkan, bukannya menggali keseluruhan tapak pelupusan dan memulihkan tanah itu kepada keadaan asal.
“Mahkamah yang membuat penilaian terikat kepada terma kontrak yang dilanggar,” katanya.

Beliau berkata kaedah penutupan dengan tanah yang dipersetujui dalam kontrak tidak boleh digantikan dengan kerja kejuruteraan yang jauh berbeza sehingga menelan kos hampir 40 kali ganda daripada anggaran asal.

Mahkamah turut mengambil kira bahawa NBC Land membeli tanah seluas 161 ekar itu pada Jun 2000 dengan harga RM32.27 juta atas dasar “seadanya”, dengan mengetahui kira-kira 36 ekar daripadanya pernah digunakan sebagai tapak pelupusan sampah majlis.
Muniandy turut memutuskan faedah sebelum penghakiman tidak wajar diberikan kerana NBC Land belum melaksanakan kerja pemulihan berkenaan atau membuat bayaran kepada kontraktor untuk melaksanakannya.
Katanya, memberikan faedah atas anggaran kos yang belum dibelanjakan juga akan memberi keuntungan tidak wajar kepada NBC Land.
Mahkamah menggantikan award Mahkamah Tinggi dengan ganti rugi RM3 juta, iaitu bahagian 50% yang dipersetujui perlu ditanggung majlis daripada keseluruhan kos pemulihan RM6 juta.
Mahkamah turut memerintahkan faedah selepas penghakiman pada kadar 5% setahun sehingga jumlah itu dibayar sepenuhnya.
Tommy Thomas, Nik Suhaimi Nik Sulaiman, Mervyn Lai, Fadzil Amin Yusoff dan Atiqah Azman mewakili majlis, manakala Cecil Abraham, Harold Tan, Lee Sin Yee dan Liu Poh Yeng mewakili NBC Land.
9bc57533f1ff8c56: PETALING JAYA: The Shah Alam High Court has rejected a former tourism agency manager’s appeal to begin serving his seven-year prison sentence for shooting his ex-wife from the date of his arrest in 2024.

Berita Harian reported today that Hafizul Hawari, 39, must serve the seven-year term after completing a six-year prison term imposed by the Kota Bharu sessions court in Kelantan for separate offences.
In his grounds of judgment dated Oct 19, Justice Shamsulbahri Ibrahim upheld the Sepang sessions court’s decision on Dec 5 last year.
Hafizul pleaded guilty to the attempted murder of Farah Isa, 40, and causing grievous hurt to the victim’s bodyguard, Nur Hadith Zaini, at KLIA Terminal 1 on April 14, 2024.
He was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment for attempted murder and seven years for causing grievous hurt with a dangerous weapon, with both sentences to run concurrently.

Last year, the Kota Bharu sessions court sentenced Hafizul to six years’ imprisonment for seven offences, including illegally possessing an Austrian Glock 19 pistol, 33 bullets, firecrackers and identity cards belonging to three other individuals, as well as driving a vehicle with a fake number plate.
He began serving the six-year sentence on the date of his arrest, April 15, 2024.
In his appeal, Hafizul did not challenge his conviction or sentence but argued that his sentence for the shooting should begin from the date of his arrest.

His lawyer, Nik Faris Syazwan Zainuzzaman, argued that Hafizul had been held in remand without bail from April 15, 2024, to Dec 5, 2025, a period of nearly 20 months that should be considered when determining the start date of his sentence.
Nik Faris said the sessions court judge failed to consider important mitigating factors, including Hafizul’s early guilty plea, lack of previous convictions and remorse for his offences.

However, Shamsulbahri said determining when the prison sentence should begin fell within the judge’s discretion and should be based on the facts of the case, the seriousness of the offence and public interest.

He ruled that the sessions court’s order was legally sound, fair and in line with Section 292 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which regulates the commencement of a new prison sentence for a person already serving a prison term.
According to the facts of the case, Farah arrived at KLIA Terminal 1 at 1.09am on April 14, 2024, after returning from the umrah with Nur Hadith.
Hafizul, who was waiting for Farah near a pillar by the lift on level three of the main terminal, fired several shots at both victims.

Nur Hadith shielded Farah and was shot several times in the abdomen. The bullets passed through his body and injured his intestines, resulting in his hospitalisation at Cyberjaya Hospital for 13 days.
Hafizul fled the scene but was later arrested in Kota Bharu while driving a vehicle with a fake number plate.
a3124a59460e25b4: WASHINGTON: A trade agreement between the United States and Canada would be reached "pretty soon," President Donald Trump told a campaign rally on Sunday, nine days ahead of crucial US midterm elections.
Tensions between the North American neighbours have been high since trade talks broke down in August, with Trump imposing a slew of new tariffs in response.

"We'll have that settled pretty soon. They're willing to give us anything at this moment," the president said of an agreement during the rally in Port Huron, a Michigan town on the US-Canada border hit hard by his tariff war.
Trump once again defended his levies on Canada and accused it of "ripping off the United States for years."
The tariffs enforced after the August talks broke down impacted around US$20 billion worth of goods, ranging from hockey sticks to cement.
In response, Canada imposed tolls on an equivalent amount of American products, leading Trump to retaliate with another round of levies of as much as 50% on certain goods.

The White House removed some of them on Friday, in response to a request from Senator Susan Collins who represents the border state of Maine, which has been disproportionately impacted by the trade war.
Democrats are targeting Collins's seat in their attempt to win control of the Senate from the Republicans in next Tuesday's midterms.
Since the start of his second term, Trump has upended the global trade order by imposing wide-ranging tariffs on friend and foe, saying they had been taking advantage of the United States.
He has also explicitly tied some threatened tariffs to political or foreign policy objectives.
1322678efaf002ab: PETALING JAYA: Pemimpin Bersama Lee Chean Chung menyeru Suruhanjaya Pilihan Raya (SPR) dan Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia (SPRM) menyiasat pengumuman menteri pengangkutan bahawa pemandu teksi Melaka akan menerima bantuan RM1,000 seorang menjelang PRN.

Lee berkata hasil, pendapatan daripada bidaan nombor pendaftaran kenderaan adalah hak awam dan sepatutnya disalur dalam Kumpulan Wang Disatukan mengikut prosedur, sebelum dibelanjakan melalui peruntukan diluluskan Parlimen.

Loke mengumumkan bantuan RM1,000 itu semasa majlis pengumuman calon PH di Melaka pada Sabtu lalu, sambil menyatakan pembayaran akan dibuat hari ini.

Beliau menyifatkan inisiatif terbabit sebahagian usaha kerajaan persekutuan menyalurkan hasil awam dalam program yang memberi manfaat kepada rakyat Malaysia serta meringankan beban tekanan kos sara hidup.
47017d57a1e8fa7f: PUTRAJAYA: The Court of Appeal has reduced a RM117 million damages award against the Klang municipal council to RM3 million in a dispute over the rehabilitation of a former municipal dumpsite.

A three-member bench chaired by Justice Ismail Brahim, sitting with Justices K Muniandy and Dean Wayne Daly, unanimously allowed the appeal by the Klang municipal council, now known as the Klang city council, against the damages awarded to property developer NBC Land Sdn Bhd.
Muniandy delivered the court’s grounds of judgment.
The court also set aside nearly RM50 million in pre-judgment interest awarded by the Shah Alam High Court and ordered NBC Land to pay RM60,000 in costs for the appeal and assessment proceedings.
The dispute arose from an agreement dated Dec 2, 2003, in which both parties agreed to share equally the estimated RM6 million cost of rehabilitating the dumpsite through soil capping.

However, the High Court assessed the overall rehabilitation cost at RM234 million, including the excavation and removal of nearly two million tonnes of waste and the replacement of the excavated material with engineered fill.
The council was ordered to pay half the amount, or RM117 million, together with interest.
In allowing the appeal, the Court of Appeal held that the assessment had gone beyond the scope of the original agreement.
Muniandy said the parties agreed to cover the waste with about 1.5m of compacted soil, not to excavate the entire landfill and restore the land to its original condition.
"The assessing court is bound to operate strictly within the four corners of the contract breached," he said.
He said the soil-capping scheme in the agreement could not be replaced with a substantially different engineering operation costing almost 40 times the original estimate.
The court also noted that NBC Land bought the 161-acre estate in June 2000 for RM32.27 million on an "as is where is" basis, knowing that about 36 acres had been used as a municipal dumpsite.
Muniandy ruled that pre-judgment interest was unjustified because NBC Land had neither carried out the rehabilitation works nor paid contractors to do so.
Awarding interest on the unspent estimated cost would also result in an impermissible windfall, he said.

The court substituted the High Court’s award with RM3 million in damages, representing the council’s agreed 50% share of the RM6 million rehabilitation cost. It also ordered post-judgment interest of 5% per annum until full settlement.
Tommy Thomas, Nik Suhaimi Nik Sulaiman, Mervyn Lai, Fadzil Amin Yusoff and Atiqah Azman appeared for the council while Cecil Abraham, Harold Tan, Lee Sin Yee and Liu Poh Yeng represented NBC Land.

832e71d4130a4024: SINGAPORE: Singapore is diversifying suppliers, adding storage and building new infrastructure to try to protect itself from growing risks of resource nationalism, Singapore’s minister for energy, trade and industry Tan See Leng said in a speech on Monday.
The remarks came as Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to the city-state from Saturday, as President Prabowo Subianto seeks to bolster domestic supply.
Singapore’s energy market authority has said the country has sufficient supplies and that the cuts represent less than 2% of its total daily gas demand, and Tan said there is no concern of shortages.

“We can keep calm and carry on,” he said at the Singapore International Energy Week conference. “Our households and our businesses can be assured that our energy security is always at the top of our minds.”

Singapore plans to add more liquefied natural gas capacity to import from a wider array of suppliers, build new power plants and increase fuel stockpiles to guard against potential disruptions, Tan said.

“Singapore will not be able to insulate ourselves from global or regional shocks,” he said. “When there is a supply crunch, countries may also prioritise their own domestic needs, and this trend of resource nationalism is particularly concerning.”

While Indonesia is a major gas exporter, overseas shipments have declined in recent years as a growing share of output is directed to domestic use. Major liquefied natural gas markets include China, Japan and South Korea, while pipeline natural gas is sent to Singapore and Malaysia.

Indonesia is a top supplier of gas to Singapore - which depends on the imported fuel for nearly all of its power generation - but the island has significantly reduced its dependence on pipeline supplies in recent years as LNG shipments have grown.
“About half of our gas is imported as LNG from a global diversified portfolio of sources, such as the US, Africa, the Middle East, and Australia,” Tan said.
The country expects to increase its LNG throughput capacity by another 50% once its second import terminal comes online ahead of 2030, he said.
The country announced plans to build five new power plants coming online between 2026 and 2031 that will increase generation capacity by more than a quarter.
Tan separately announced a non-binding agreement between Saudi Arabia and the city-state to store Saudi crude oil in caverns beneath Jurong Island from the second half of 2027.
4ebf17daf3222bea: UK retail giant Tesco appears to have decided to replace VMware with Proxmox in its stores.

A job ad for a new Head of Software Engineering: Edge Platform role says the gig involves leading “two major, interconnected engineering priorities: modernising Tesco’s edge virtualisation estate through the migration from VMware to Proxmox, and building a robust, scalable software-driven Edge Management Platform to provision, manage, monitor and maintain the retail edge estate throughout its lifecycle.”
The stakes are high because the job ad says Tesco’s Edge Platform “provides the underlying computing environment and software capabilities that enable applications to run across our stores.”

“Store technology must remain dependable despite connectivity disruptions, constrained local resources and the complexity of managing software and infrastructure changes across thousands of locations. Failures or poorly executed changes can directly affect store operations, colleague productivity and customer experience.”

Whoever scores the job will “own the engineering strategy and execution of Tesco’s migration from VMware to Proxmox across the edge estate, delivering a secure, reliable and cost-effective alternative virtualisation platform” - and do it from Bengaluru, India.
One KPI is “Safe and predictable migration from VMware to Proxmox, successful validation of required store configurations, reduced legacy dependencies and effective operational handover.”

In case you came in late, Proxmox is an open-source virtualization platform offered by an Austrian company. The product has gained considerable interest as a VMware alternative for edge, hyperconverged, and basic server virtualization scenarios. Proxmox is trying to grow into a full software-defined datacenter contender, too.

Independent analyst Michael Warrilow rates [PDF] Proxmox as technically strong but warns would-be users will need to find a support partner because until recently the company only offered support during business hours in Austria. That changed in September when Proxmox announced 24/7 support for enterprise customers.
In an email to The Register, Warrilow said “Modernisation is the key to reducing the dependence on VMware: reduce legacy whilst adding incremental value to a new initiative.”
“Supermarkets and general merchandise are ripe for this, more so given they are a location where VMware had more competition and less differentiation.”

“The Tesco job spec has many of the ingredients for a next-gen, cloud-inspired instore experience,” he added. “API-driven, ‘programmable’ infrastructure that allows rapid deployment and a better experience for customers.”
Tesco operates over 5,000 stores around the world. We’ve asked the retail giant to enumerate the extent of its planned Proxmox rollout.
Scuttlebutt suggests Tesco will adopt Microsoft’s Hyper-V for its core workloads. VMware, however, has indicated to The Register it does not consider Tesco a lost cause.

Tesco is making the move after suing VMware over a contract dispute. The retailer claims VMware is bound to support software it acquired under a perpetual license, and to upgrade some software. The virtualization giant retorted that it no longer makes the software Tesco wants to upgrade to. Tesco says that during negotiations, VMware made an offer that represented a 175 percent price increase.
The matter remains before the courts, with hearings likely in 2027.
VMware’s dispute with several Siemens companies also continues. In that case, VMware alleged Siemens abused copyright by using more software than its licenses permitted.

Siemens’ parent company, Siemens AG, appears to have recently exited the case, an important change as it is Germany-based and the case is being heard in the USA. The remaining defendants last week filed a defence that denies VMware’s claims.

In better news for VMware, it last week announced a ten-year agreement with Japanese carrier NTT Docomo and a continued engagement at transport giant FedEx. Both companies will use VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation private cloud bundle to power their operations. ®
feba17b888ed755d: BHUBANESWAR: Two states along India's eastern coast were preparing to evacuate thousands of people ahead of Cyclone Arnab, which is expected to make landfall on Wednesday, as one of them said it would close schools in some districts for two days.

Arnab, which formed over the Bay of Bengal before intensifying into a cyclonic storm, is expected to make landfall in Andhra Pradesh state by Wednesday morning, with gustsof as much as 140 kph (87 mph), India's weather office said.
The cyclone will probably intensify further, it added.
The weather system is expected to bring heavy to extremely heavy rainfall to Andhra Pradesh's northern and central coastal districts, and southern regions of neighbouring Odisha.
Andhra Pradesh has called for boats at sea to return ashore and ordered speedy restoration of power in case of disruptions.
A senior Andhra Pradesh disaster management official told Reuters on Monday the state government had identified 570,000 people as vulnerable and evacuations would start on Monday evening.
Odisha's government announced the closure of schools and colleges in five districts for Tuesday and Wednesday, and said it was preparing to move residents of low-lying areas to cyclone shelters.
The Bay of Bengal is one of the world's major regions for tropical cyclones.
f246629971f54217: SHAH ALAM, Oct 26 — The Selangor state government will not tolerate the use of any place of worship for criminal purposes, regardless of the religion, race or background of those involved.

Selangor Human Resources and Poverty Eradication Committee chairman V. Papparaidu said he took seriously media reports about drugs being found at an unregistered place of worship in Klang during an operation by the Selangor Narcotics Criminal Investigation Department from Oct 13 to 19.
“This case underscores the need for strict enforcement to combat drug distribution and the misuse of premises.

“Places of worship should be respected, kept sacred and provide peace to their respective congregations, not be used to store prohibited substances or facilitate criminal activities,” he said in a statement today.

Papparaidu, also co-chairman of the Special Committee on Buddhist, Christian, Hindu, Sikh and Taoist Affairs, stressed that there would be no compromise on using places of worship for criminal purposes.

“However, we must distinguish between the criminal actions of individuals and the religious institutions and communities they belong to. The actions of a few individuals should not be used as a reason to vilify or stigmatise an entire religious community,” he said.
He said the matter had nothing to do with religion or race, but concerned the rule of law, public safety and respect for the sanctity of places of worship.

“Criminal activities must be dealt with according to the evidence and the law, rather than sentiments or prejudices directed at any particular community,” he said, expressing support for the police in conducting a thorough investigation and taking appropriate action against those involved.
Selangor police busted a drug trafficking operation that allegedly used an unregistered place of worship in Klang as a storage facility, following raids across the state. — Bernama

2d35a610f1c4edfa: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — The Higher Education Ministry (MoHE) has stressed that students living in rented accommodation off campus should inform their universities of their place of residence to facilitate monitoring.
Its minister, Datuk Seri Dr Zambry Abd Kadir, said monitoring was difficult because some students arranged their own rental accommodation without going through their universities.

“So, that makes it rather difficult for us to monitor them. What we emphasise, however, is that they should always inform us of their whereabouts and where they are staying,” he said during the question-and-answer session in the Dewan Rakyat today.

He was responding to a supplementary question from Dr Ahmad Fakhruddin Fakhrurazi (PN-Kuala Kedah) on the ministry’s proposal to work with state governments and property owners to provide student rental accommodation at controlled rates near public higher education institutions (IPTAs), pending the completion of new residential colleges.

Zambry said some public universities and polytechnics worked with their student affairs divisions to manage accommodation in designated areas, while some students opted to rent accommodation independently.

He said the proposal to provide student rental accommodation at controlled rates was also being considered to meet undergraduates’ housing needs, but its implementation would depend on the capacity of the universities concerned and their financial positions.
The proposal had also been raised by student representative councils, with several universities identified as requiring greater attention and priority in terms of student accommodation.

On targeted rental assistance for B40 students who failed to secure places in residential colleges, Zambry said priority was given to this group, along with students with disabilities, athletes and uniformed corps members, for hostel accommodation.

In reply to the original question from Datuk Seri Dr Wan Azizah Wan Ismail (PH-Bandar Tun Razak) on efforts to address the shortage of accommodation at IPTAs, he said the government was working with government-linked investment companies (GLICs) to develop student accommodation facilities.
These included the Universiti Malaya Student Residence, which is expected to be completed in 2031 and benefit 10,000 students.

In addition, Budget 2027 announced a RM750 million allocation by the Retirement Fund (Incorporated) (KWAP) for the development of the Vista Kampus project at Universiti Sultan Zainal Abidin (UniSZA) and Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM), before it is expanded to six other universities.

Responding to a supplementary question from Dr Wan Azizah on incentives for the private sector to develop residential colleges, Zambry said MoHE, Finance Ministry, KWAP and the Public Private Partnership Unit (UKAS) were discussing ways to strengthen a hybrid public-private partnership (PPP) approach. — Bernama

575dcdbed5ce17d7: Internet governance bodies are likely to accelerate work to prepare the domain name system (DNS) so it can remain secure once quantum computers can challenge conventional encryption.

John Crain, ICANN’s chief technology officer, last week told The Register that he is aware of efforts within the organization, and at other internet governance bodies, to consider what happens once commercially available quantum computers become capable of easily deciphering encrypted information.
Those machines theoretically pose a risk to DNSSEC, the Domain Name System Security Extensions that adapt PKI to the job of verifying the veracity of DNS records.
The CTO said he’s aware of predictions that such computers could come online “at the turn of the decade” and that he has therefore changed his view of when the DNS needs to be made quantum safe.

“If you asked me years ago, I would have said we probably need to be ready in ten years,” Crain said. “Now, maybe it's less than that. I don't know if it's three years or five, but it's probably not ten”.
One way to quantum-proof DNSSEC is to use larger keys that even a quantum computer will struggle to crack. Doing so, however, runs into message size limits in the DNS.

“If we go for larger key sizes, that means larger zones, larger packets, larger responses,” Crain said. It can also mean traffic being carried by multiple TCP packets, instead of the single UDP messages DNS prefers.
Crain said ICANN, the IETF, and other internet governance bodies are aware of this challenge and have begun preliminary work to address it.

“Being prepared to go from UDP to TCP is going to take a few years,” he told The Register at ICANN’s annual meeting in Bali last week. “We're probably a few years away from being able to deploy in a predictable manner.”
The internet community has, however, seen that the problem is becoming more acute.
“We're going to ramp up the speed of development,” Crain said.
Internet registry reform nears

At ICANN’s Bali conference, The Register also met Jia-Rong Low, in his capacity as chair of the Number Resource Organization, the peak body for the world’s five regional internet registries (RIRs), AFRINIC, APNIC, ARIN, LACNIC, and RIPE NCC.

The topic of that conversation was Internet Coordination Policy 2 (ICP-2), the document that governs RIRs. In its current form, ICP-2 describes the formation of a new RIR but no other part of its operations.

After strife at AFRINIC raised the possibility of the African registry failing, the NRO decided to update ICP-2 so it covered the entire lifecycle of an RIR, from formation through to possible derecognition.

Work on ICP-2 has moved through several rounds of public consultation. It has reached the status of a recommended draft. Low told The Register work on the document has proven “very challenging” to develop entirely with remote work. Last week’s ICANN meeting, he said, offered a venue for in-person collaboration that he hopes will result in work accelerating.

The revised document defines four stages in the life of an RIR: recognition, audit, emergency continuity operations, and derecognition. The last three are additions to ICP-2 and give ICANN a major role as an independent overseer of RIRs.
Low is hopeful a final document will be ready for review by the end of 2026, and ready for implementation not long afterwards.
Scammers target trustworthy-sounding domains like .bank or .pharmacy
Phisherfolk and other scammy scum strive to register authoritative-sounding domains as part of their efforts to trick victims.

ICANN defines some global top level domains (GTLDs) as “Category 1” strings, because they pertain to regulated sectors – such as .bank, .doctor, and .university – or are felt to need special safeguards because like .sucks they create the potential for bullying.

In a session at the ICANN meeting, Siôn Lloyd, ICANN’s principal security, stability and resiliency scientist, said the organization has investigated whether certain top level domains attract more abuse.

He found that Category 1 GTLDs are more likely to be targeted by DNS abusers and therefore have a 45 percent higher chance of abuse than other domains. Happily, Category 1 domains are also less likely to have high abuse volumes.

ICANN is currently working on a policy (PDP1) that will require domain registrars to take extra action against owners of domains that facilitate abuse, and another (PDP2) that will regulate automated domain registration.
More GTLDs, more often?

The Register heard plenty of chat at the meeting about ICANN’s new round of applications for GTLDs, which seems to be progressing well. Across various panels and sessions, we also heard references to ICANN’s past statements that new GTLD application rounds should be more frequent and take place at a predictable cadence, along with some suggestions that this round of applications is the template for future rounds. ®
99c40e483384af3d: Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written. The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome. At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life. On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president. A night of firsts The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways. First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win. Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks. Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history. Only Getúlio Vargas governed longer. He held power for almost two decades through a revolution, dictatorship and democratic election from the 1930–50s, and is widely considered Brazil’s most consequential president. Third, no runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media, supporting both sides. Unlike the first round, the second round was not quiet, nor was it decided by television ads. Brazil saw a mass mobilization of voters, and it was ferocious. The Brazilian left fought an uphill battle against social media platforms, economic elites, and a Supreme Electoral Court whose president was accused of trying to tip the balance to favour Bolsonaro. Lula has a long record of political miracles, and he has added another one to the list. An election result that matters beyond Brazil Lula’s victory matters well beyond Brazil’s borders, also in three ways. Globally, Brazil remains a bulwark against the rise of the far right. In recent elections across Latin America and Europe, far-right parties and leaders have advanced almost everywhere. Brazil, the world’s fourth-largest democracy, has now bucked the trend, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore. Regionally, Lula has defied the so-called “incumbent curse”. Over the past decade in Latin America, governing parties have lost election after election, punished by voters for inflation, insecurity and economic stagnation. Brazil’s economy was in reasonable shape, but its gains were modest and unevenly felt. Everything pointed to a defeat, and Lula beat the odds anyway. His win is also a check on what critics have called the “Donroe Doctrine”, referring to the Trump administration’s push to bring the Western Hemisphere more firmly into the US sphere of influence through tariffs, threats and political patronage. Bolsonaro had campaigned as Washington’s preferred partner in South America. Brazil’s voters turned that offer down. Domestically, the result also shows the power of popular mobilisation on the left. After Lula’s poor first-round showing, Lula’s campaign re-energised demoralised supporters and built a broad coalition of voters, some of whom were voting less for Lula than against what Bolsonaro represents. It also mobilised people who had stayed home in the first round to get out to vote. The battle is not over Lula should not mistake survival for vindication. Yes, he corrected course. In three weeks, he acknowledged the mistakes he made over four years in office, especially during a lacklustre first-round campaign. He sharpened his message, widened his alliances and spoke directly to the voters he had lost. That is no small achievement for a politician, however experienced he may be. But he now has to govern a country more polarised than ever. Political violence on the streets has increased, and hate speech circulates freely online. Prominent figures on the far right, including Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, have already said they will not accept this election result. Bolsonaro said late Sunday he will not concede, and will seek an annulment of the vote. And then there is Washington. Given the White House’s close ties to the Bolsonaro family, there is a real risk the Trump administration will question, or even refuse to recognise, the outcome of the election. That would be extraordinary, and a few years ago, it would have been unthinkable. Things are further complicated by a legal battle on election day itself. After allegations of voter suppression of Lula’s supporters in several cities, the justices of Brazil’s Supreme Court and Supreme Electoral Court clashed over whether to extend voting hours. Whatever the legal merits, the dispute gives the losing side a ready-made narrative of “voting irregularities”. This could be a matter of serious concern, and it may last for weeks. Three questions for Lula’s next term When Lula is inaugurated on January 5, three questions will define his fourth term. The first is how Lula will govern a deeply divided country with a conservative majority in Congress and over a dozen right-wing state governors. The legislature that held him hostage over the past four years has grown more hostile, not less. Every budget, every reform and every appointment will be a tough negotiation, with the possibility of an impeachment hanging over Lula’s head. The second is repair. How will he deal with problems that go well beyond partisan disputes? These include fiscal pressures from rising government spending, a steady loss of trust in democratic institutions, and an institutional system that no longer works as designed. The Supreme Court, once the guarantor of the democratic order, has seen its legitimacy eroded by a major financial scandal surrounding Banco Master. Although the president cannot “repair” a court, he can refuse to treat the crisis as someone else’s problem. The third question is the most important. Will Lula, his Workers’ Party (PT) and Brazil’s broader democratic forces use this reprieve to renew Brazilian politics? That would mean: new political leadership alternatives beyond the ageing leaders who have dominated the left for 40 years new forms of popular political participation that do not depend on a single charismatic figure a new narrative that speaks to the precarious workers, religious families and angry voters who have drifted toward the far right. This is the only real antidote to polarisation, and it will not come from a single election or a single leader. Lula’s comeback has bought Brazil time. Whether it buys anything more depends on what he and his allies do over the next four years, one step at a time. Lula has worked another miracle. His last task is to make sure Brazil does not need another one. 8166ea01030596b6: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — Malaysia is well positioned to play a key role as a regional data centre hub if it can maintain its competitive advantage, Moody’s Ratings said.
It said Malaysia’s competitive advantage stems from competitively priced, readily available power and supportive government initiatives.

Moody’s Ratings assistant vice president - ratings Chelsia Ng said the country’s policy framework and approval requirements already focus on data centre efficiency, with eligibility for tax incentives under the Digital Ecosystem Acceleration (DESAC) scheme linked to power and water efficiency benchmarks.
“Johor, which houses most of the country’s data centre capacity, also applies more stringent requirements for project approvals.

“These measures should promote more efficient resource use, which should help moderate the incremental pressure on power and water infrastructure as the sector grows,” Ng told Bernama in a recent interview.

Moody’s Ratings estimated that around 14 gigawatts (GW) to 17 GW of additional generation capacity will be required by 2035 to meet the incremental demand in Peninsular Malaysia, which could entail around RM80 billion to RM95 billion of investments to be undertaken by Tenaga Nasional Bhd (TNB) and independent power producers.

Ng noted that data centre-led demand growth would be credit-positive for utilities over the long term, but the elevated capital spending would also entail execution and funding risks and raise financial leverage during the development phase.
She noted that based on government projections, data centres could account for around 31 per cent of total electricity consumption in Peninsular Malaysia by 2035, up from 4.0 per cent in 2025.

“This will underpin structural electricity demand growth, and we expect demand in Peninsular Malaysia to grow at a compound annual rate of around 5.8 per cent over the next decade, although the scale and pace of growth will remain subject to market and execution risks,” said Ng.

She noted that the need for firm baseload capacity to meet data centre power demand would keep gas relevant as a transition fuel, whilst Malaysia continues to scale up solar capacity and battery energy storage systems (BESS) to support system reliability.
Ng said the procurement of new and extended gas-fired capacity under NewGen25 and NewGen26 also underscores the importance of gas in maintaining system reliability as electricity demand rises.

“However, Malaysia will need to balance this requirement (to phase) down coal generation and the need to replace retiring generation capacities over the next decade, which will add another layer of investment and execution risk to the energy transition,” she added.

Ng said renewable energy (RE) could also meet part of the additional electricity demand, as solar capacity could be deployed relatively quickly, adding that data centre operators also have their own net-zero and decarbonisation targets, which could drive demand for RE-linked power procurement over time.

Although solar remains a modest contributor to Peninsular Malaysia’s generation mix, she noted that the mandatory inclusion of BESS in the recently launched large-scale solar (LSS) tender programme points to the growing role for solar-plus-storage in meeting incremental demand while supporting Malaysia’s decarbonisation initiatives.

“However, the intermittent nature of renewable generation and current battery storage technologies are unlikely to provide sufficient backup to fully meet data centres’ round-the-clock power requirements in the medium term,” she added.

In June, the government announced that Malaysia will require all future solar power projects under its sixth LSS programme to include BESS, as the government moves to strengthen grid stability alongside RE expansion.

Ng noted that data centre-led demand growth would be credit positive for utilities over the long term, but the elevated capital spending would also entail execution and funding risks and raise financial leverage during the development phase.
“For TNB, annual capital spending is likely to increase to around RM18 billion, driven by higher investment in grid infrastructure and generation capacity.
“Its regulated transmission and distribution investments benefit from a cost-recovery framework which underpins revenue growth,” she added.

Although unregulated generation projects carry greater risk because they take longer to build before generating cash flow, Moody’s Ratings expects TNB to have sufficient financial headroom to manage sizable capital spending over the medium term. — Bernama

90e03c134e74b890: WASHINGTON: A wave of American wealth created by artificial intelligence companies could produce some of the largest charitable sums since the era of Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller, raising questions about where the money goes.

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, has said it would commit 5% of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a stake that could be worth around US$100 billion if the company reaches the US$2 trillion valuation investors are eyeing for a stock market debut expected as early as November.

Combined with pledges by its seven co-founders to give away 80% of their equity and a program matching employees’ donations, Anthropic says roughly a fifth of its shares will be dedicated to public-benefit purposes.
"This might be one of the biggest stories in corporate philanthropy ever," said Michael Moody, a professor of philanthropic studies at Indiana University’s Lilly Family School of Philanthropy.

The OpenAI Foundation, the nonprofit that controls ChatGPT maker OpenAI, holds a 26% stake in the company that was valued at about US$130 billion when it was restructured a year ago, more than the endowment of the Gates Foundation.

Nan Ransohoff of payments firm Stripe has described the moment as a "third wave" of American philanthropy, after the industrial fortunes of the late 19th century and the internet billionaires of recent decades.
'Dies disgraced'
Carnegie argued in his 1889 essay "The Gospel of Wealth" that "the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced," and by his death had given away the bulk of his fortune, about US$350 million.
Carnegie transferred what remained into a trust, which has continued to make grants for more than a century.
Rockefeller's money built universities and funded medical research and public health campaigns around the world.
Railroad magnate Cornelius Vanderbilt gave comparatively little, apart from the US$1 million that founded the university bearing his name.

Anthropic is setting up its fund as a limited liability company that it wholly owns, rather than as a nonprofit foundation, which must pay out a minimum share of its assets each year and file public tax returns.

"The trade-off is that decision-making stays with the company and transparency is voluntary," said Sarah Wolfolds, who studies nonprofit organizations at Cornell University's SC Johnson College of Business.
Anthropic has said the fund's equity will not be used for lobbying or political giving and that it will report on its activities.
'Where the money is'
Many Anthropic founders and staff have close ties to effective altruism, a movement that favors causes such as AI safety and global health because of their measurable impact.
"Nonprofits tend to reorient their programs toward where the money is," Wolfolds said, warning that other causes can become neglected.
Moody said the philanthropic world would be "looking closely at which causes they support," including whether research funding is limited to AI.
Laura McGarry, of fundraising consultancy Graham-Pelton, said the charities best placed to benefit are those that already have relationships with the newly wealthy.
"It’s really about values alignment," she said, adding that charities that court the newly rich only after their big payday risk looking transactional.
Effective altruism has shaped some donors' giving but has not "dramatically upset the apple cart," she said.
Anthropic has said the fund could make payments directly to groups affected by AI's impact on jobs, without giving details.
Research on cash transfers is encouraging, Wolfolds said, but "the harder challenge may be identifying who has been affected by AI."
Such payments should complement, not replace, unemployment insurance and retraining programs, she said.
One child, one share
Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, whose SpaceX owns rival AI developer xAI, criticized Anthropic’s approach.
"I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," he wrote on X.
As an alternative, Musk pledged one of his SpaceX shares to every American child next year, a gift worth about US$10.5 billion.

US President Donald Trump praised the move as fitting the philosophy behind his "Trump Accounts," government-backed investment accounts for children born between 2025 and 2028. Billionaires Michael and Susan Dell have pledged billions to the program.
4876528c8865a1cc: FRANKFURT: France's deteriorating public finances will take centre stage when the European Central Bank meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone's second-biggest economy just yet.

The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.

But the focus of Thursday's meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis," said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.

French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year's budget, which aims to reduce the country's vast debts.
Concerns have also been fuelled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combatting sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields.
However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France's problems do not meet the threshold.

The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted" moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading - but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB president Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France's finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea.
Asked about France's rising yields earlier this month, she responded: "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
France's central bank chief, who sits on the ECB's governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met" for the central bank to step in.

Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France" at Thursday's meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Rates on hold
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5%.
The ECB's rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the US central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September.
Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8% in September, although closely watched core inflation - excluding volatile energy and food prices - hardly changed.
There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices," ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France's crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike," he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB's task".
Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year.
She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos.
But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB's last meeting in September there was "nothing to report" on the matter.
